facts.claim: "Lying To Your Face" by Evan Honer & Sierra Carson was released January 30, 2026 by Cloverdale Records on the album Everything I Wanted (& more). It runs 3:05.
The song is written by Evan Honer and Sierra Carson.
Evan Honer and Shane Travis are credited as producers of the track.
The song is one of three new tracks on the deluxe edition, alongside "Die a Drunk" and "For Myself". The edition also adds two reimagined tracks.

The Everything I Wanted project was made in a garage studio with close collaborators Shane Travis and Garrett Hall, plus other musician friends. This is the project's recording setup as described in press. It is not stated specifically for this track.
Honer told PEOPLE the deluxe release is the end of the Everything I Wanted chapter. He also said the album's story is about finally giving love a shot.
Honer founded and runs Cloverdale Records, an artist-driven label. Sierra Carson is on its roster.
Honer's touring band includes Shane Travis (electric guitar), Brian Kabala (keys), Tyson Rodgers (drums), Ian Malinowski (bass) and Conner West (pedal steel, banjo, guitar).

Honer is a Nashville-based singer-songwriter who blends folk, country and indie rock. His earlier albums are Jersey Giant (2022), West on I-10 (2023) and Fighting For (2024). The third album, Everything I Wanted, came out September 19, 2025.
Honer is a former diver who graduated from California Baptist University in 2022. He releases music on his self-published label Cloverdale Records.

research.lineage: It sits in the modern Nashville-based alt-country/folk and indie-rock singer-songwriter scene, on an artist-run independent label, and one review says Honer is moving from folk and country toward indie rock.

draft:
The most deflating line in **Lying To Your Face** is also the funniest. The chorus builds a superhero: if you need saving, the singer will suit up. Then it lands on the question that undoes all of it: "you'll still ask 'why were you late.'" It's the gap between grand devotion and a small, nagging doubt, and anyone who has loved someone who can't quite believe them knows exactly how that sounds across a kitchen.

Evan Honer and Sierra Carson wrote it together, and the writing is smarter than a standard he-said, she-said duet. The first verse is a complaint. Everyone the narrator knows would walk away, and still the partner keeps asking if they're leaving. The second verse flips the pronouns and makes the narrator the anxious one. Everyone they've loved has walked away, so now they're the one asking, and they admit it: "it's a pattern I've been trying hard to shake." The accusation in the title turns out to run both ways. Each person is defending against a fear they're also guilty of. The song lets frustration and self-recognition sit next to each other without deciding who's right.

The best image carries that double meaning too: "I'd swim oceans with an anchor round my waist." It sounds like a vow, but it's also a picture of drowning. Love here is a feat of strength performed while something drags you down. The bridge offers the only real way out, a deal rather than a rescue: I won't go if you won't go. Then something small happens in the last chorus. The "if" drops away. The earlier hypothetical, that love might not be enough, now comes out flat, as a plain statement.

The sound stays out of the way. A fingerpicked acoustic pattern and a simple, sustained bass line set the floor. Drums come in with kick, snare and hi-hat before a ride cymbal opens things up, all at a relaxed, steady walk. The lead voice is clear and a little nasal, sung like conversation. The second voice joins in harmony, and the shift from one voice to two does the work the lyrics describe. Honer and Shane Travis produced it with a clean, polished finish and a modest room around it.

It's one of three new songs added to the deluxe edition of Everything I Wanted, on Cloverdale Records, the artist-run label Honer founded and where Carson is signed. Honer has called the album a story about finally giving love a shot, and he says this edition closes that chapter. This song is that story with the hard part left in. It belongs to the Nashville folk-and-country songwriter scene that keeps leaning toward indie rock, though here the leaning is gentle.

What sticks is that line about being late: the song makes you feel how exhausting it is to keep proving yourself, and then quietly admits you're doing the same thing to them.
